hook: In 1885, Finland built a lighthouse on the Swedish half of an island.
twist: The border across Märket, a bare Baltic skerry, ran straight through its midpoint from 1809. Finland's 1885 lighthouse stood 35-60 m inside Sweden, and the official papers do not say why. In 1985 the two countries moved the border, not the lighthouse: 3,913 square metres swapped each way, leaving a zigzag border on a rock nobody lives on.
angle: Why does a border zigzag across a rock in the sea? Paper lighthouse, a ruler line through the middle, then the swap of two equal pieces animated on a real OSM outline of the island.
why_now: Evergreen (no dated hook; timeliness scored 1). Evidence from the YouTube scout (docs/research/topics/why-map-2026-10-06.json): 'The Strangest Border Between Sweden & Finland, Märket Island' (GeoGlobeTales) 29.7M views, the 16th most-viewed of 439 Shorts in the niche; 'The Strangest Borders in the World' (Geo Bytes) 4.1M, outlier 42, also features a Finland-Sweden border oddity. Our fresh detail: the Swedish parliament's 1985 report says the reason for the misplaced lighthouse is not on record, and gives the exact 3,913 m2 swap.
risks: Popular retellings say the lighthouse was built there 'by mistake'; the primary source only says the reason is not recorded. Say 'the papers don't say why', never 'by mistake'.
Finland was a Grand Duchy under the Russian Empire in 1885; the Riksdag report says 'Finland' built it, so the script says Finland.
